title: New-home builders report regulatory and permit delay, but permit approval time itself is not measured in the sources read

history.reason: Weak signal: builder-reported delay from an advocacy-group survey; Census-based data show a short post-permit wait and do not measure approval time.

description: Single-family builders surveyed by NAHB overwhelmingly report that regulation, which can include delays in obtaining permits or inspections, delays their projects; but the readable data measure builder-perceived delay and post-permit start lag, not permit application-to-issuance time or friction specific to small builders and remodelers.
customer_segment: Single-family home builders (NAHB HMI panel, stratified by size); small builders and remodelers are the intended segment but are not separately measured in the sources read.
geography: United States (national averages; regional variation reported)
context: Evidence dated March 2026 (NAHB surveys) and calendar 2025 (Census-based timing). Local permit processes differ by jurisdiction; no jurisdiction-level performance report was read.

evidence.text: 93.4% of surveyed builders (n=337) reported regulation caused some construction-process delay, averaging a little over six weeks where present; the question includes unreasonable delays in obtaining permits or inspections.
94.2% of surveyed developers (n=54) reported regulatory delay averaging roughly seven months.
NAHB estimates the pure cost of regulatory delay at $1,632 per home in construction and $2,480 in development, about 0.8% of house price combined.
Census-based data summarized by NAHB show an average 1.4 months from authorization to start of construction for single-family homes completed in 2025.
Small builders and remodelers spend material unpaid staff or owner time on permit applications, resubmittals and status chasing.

alternatives: Permit expediters and architects/engineers who file on the builder's behalf; jurisdictions' own online permit portals; not investigated.

contradictory_evidence.text: Delay costs are small relative to other regulatory items in NAHB's own estimate (about 0.8% of house price versus 26.4% total), so permit delay is not the largest burden even by the advocacy group's numbers.
Census-based timing shows only about 1.4 months from permit to start, with nearly all of that after approval; it does not show long approval waits.
Both sources come from a builders' trade association with a policy interest in showing regulatory burden; the builder delay question lumps permit and inspection delay with other regulation.

uncertainty: Unknown: application-to-issuance time and its distribution; share of delay due to applicant corrections versus agency queues; how small builders and remodelers differ from the HMI panel; any remodeling-specific data; and whether builders would pay for tools given that jurisdictions control the process.
open_questions: What do city/county permitting performance reports show for residential application-to-issuance time, and for small projects?
How much is resubmittal and correction churn versus agency queue time?
Do remodelers (not covered here) face different friction?
next_actions: Find readable jurisdiction permit-timeline dashboards or audits for residential permits.
Look for non-advocacy measurement of permit review times.
Read the Census Survey of Construction tables directly.
